column1: # cases.tsv - the assertions this suite makes, and what each one is called.
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Alexandre Gomes Gaigalas <alganet@gmail.com>
# SPDX-License-Identifier: ISC
# id <TAB> title <TAB> applies-to
# `applies-to` is a space separated list of lanes, or `*` for every lane. It is
# what turns a missing row into a reading: a case that applies to a lane and was
# never reported there is a hole, and until this file existed there was no way to
# tell that from a case nobody had written yet.
# Named lanes and not `*`, because no case here applies to all ten. With `*` the
# grid put a `-` in thirty-three cells for a lane that runs none of them, which is
# noise in the column that is supposed to carry the signal: `-` has to mean a lane
# that was expected to report and did not.
# That was written when four lanes reported nothing at all -- bsd, kde-live,
# wayland and macos-netinstall each ran one thing and none of it was this. Three
# of the four report now: they run netinstall/test/run.sh, and splash.sh speaks
# this vocabulary, so bsd, wayland and macos-netinstall carry the splash family
# below. kde-live is still the one lane with no row anywhere here; it runs
# test/qtkde.sh and nothing else, and until that suite has a vocabulary it is a
# lane the registry has nothing to say about.
# windows-launch was absent from the walk for a long time, because
# verify-windows.ps1 asserted the same facts in its own sentences and reported
# none of these ids. It is on them now: it writes the samples it was already
# taking as a record and hands that to test/lib/walk.sh, which is the shape
# verify-std.ps1 has used to reach test/lib/analyse.sh since the analysis moved
# there. Four lanes hold the walk now rather than three.
# walk.close.process-exits stays macOS's alone. It watches a *process* after the
# window is gone rather than a record, so there is nothing in the walk record for
# another lane to answer it from.
# The ids are dotted and start with the probe family, so a sheet sorts into the
# order somebody reads it in. They are stable across lanes on purpose -- three
# verifiers assert that a window reached 500x400 and until now spelled it three
# different ways, which made one fact look like three to sheetdiff.py.
# The launcher's own walk: neutrinotest.js drives it and verify-linux.sh,
# verify-macos.sh and verify-windows.ps1 each watch it on their own platform.
walk.window.appeared
column2: the app opened a window

column2: the app started and reported in

column1: # The splash window, from netinstall/test/splash.sh -- the first suite in the

# the grid at all.
# It is the whole of what the wayland lane runs (NEUTRINO_SUITES=splash) and the
# headline of macos-netinstall, so converting one file put a Wayland compositor
# and an AppKit desktop into a column that had been empty. bsd runs it too, in an
# OpenBSD guest. kde is absent on purpose: it asks the netinstall suite for `env`
# and `e2e` only, because it shares a kernel with gjs and the rest would be the
# same measurement taken twice on the same machine.
# Several of these are skips rather than failures on a lane that draws nothing,
# which is most of what this suite has to say about a machine with no display:
# there is no hold on a window that does not exist, and saying so is different

column1: # The pin and the payload, from netinstall/test/verify.sh -- the second suite in
# the netinstall tree to speak this vocabulary.
# The lane list is splash's minus wayland, and the difference is not a judgement
# about the check: wayland asks the netinstall suite for `splash` and nothing
# else, because what is being measured on that lane is a compositor. bsd runs
# these, in an OpenBSD guest, off the reduced suite list that drops the two
# suites needing a webview -- which is why converting this file deepens a column
# that until now carried one family.
# Nothing here skips. Every case is a question about a hash or a file, answerable
# on any machine with a compiler, so a `-` in one of these cells is a lane that
# went quiet rather than a lane that could not answer.
# verify.fixture.oversized is a guard rather than a claim about the binary, and
# it earns a row for the reason it exists: the oversized payload is seventeen
# megabytes of `a`, and when the fixture was silently not created -- which
# happened, on windows, where nt_python cannot open an MSYS /tmp path -- the
# rejection below it passed against a file that was not there. Measured again
# here: emptying the fixture turns both this and verify.payload.oversized red.
verify.fixture.oversized
column2: the oversized fixture was actually created

column1: # The spec grammar, from netinstall/test/names.sh -- the third netinstall suite
# through the conversion, and the first where an id is not one assertion.
# That file makes about seventy of them, and most are one spec apiece: twelve
# reserved shapes, nine malformed names, six downloader markers, six pin lengths.
# Seventy rows here would be seventy rows of `.` in six of the ten columns, and
# they would say seventy times over the one thing this suite has to say -- that
# four lanes read the grammar the same way. So an id names the question and the
# sentence keeps the spec, which is what a reader of a red lane actually needs.
# Nothing is averaged away by that. test/matrix.py resolves a repeated id by
# letting FAIL win -- it has done since decoflip started reporting one case under
# two decoration settings -- so a family whose twelfth member broke is a red
# cell. Measured rather than assumed: asserting that shape 1 is reserved, which
# it is not, turns names.shape.reserved red on a lane where its other twelve
# members passed, whichever end of the list the failure is at.
# Same lanes as verify: the netinstall suite without a shorter list named for it.
# Two of these skip on windows-launch rather than failing -- there is no name
# without .exe there to strip, and a symlink needs privilege -- which is a SKIP
# with a reason on it and not a hole.

column1: # The pin floor, from netinstall/test/pinfloor.sh. Same lanes again: the suite
# runs first in the netinstall list, and it is in the reduced OpenBSD one too,
# because a floor is a question about a parser and needs no webview.
# pinfloor.boundary is fourteen pin lengths under one id, for the reason
# names.sh groups: the sentence carries the length and the id carries the claim.
# 0, 1, 8, 15, 16, 17, 24, 31 and 65 and 80 must refuse; 32 through 64 must
# resolve. Both ends, so a floor that went up cannot pass by rejecting more than
# it was asked to -- measured by moving the expected floor to 33, which turns
# the cell red on the one length that changed.
# pinfloor.cause.distinct is the case this file is really about and it had no
# row at all before the conversion, because it spoke only when it failed. Before
# the floor moved, a pin below it was fetched and then failed the comparison --
# the same sentence a wrong pin produces -- so a suite asserting "this was
# refused" could not say which refusal it got. That it is now two refusals is
# what verify.pin.reason and names.pin.floor.reason rest on.
# The six `report:` lines this suite ends on stay readings and get no id. They
# say what the floor is rather than whether it held, and a reading in the grid
# would be a row that cannot be true or false.
pinfloor.boundary
column2: the floor accepts 32 through 64 and refuses both sides

column1: # What each platform leaves writable, from netinstall/test/writable.sh. The same

# and writable is in the reduced OpenBSD one too.
# writable.letters is one id for every target the payload plants into, grouped
# the way names.sh and pinfloor.sh group: the sentence carries the target and
# the id carries the claim. The expected set is per-platform and each lane holds
# its own, so this cell going red means one letter moved somewhere -- measured
# by flipping the Linux set's `home` to writable, which turns it red on one of
# six and leaves the rest green.
# Two of these can be skipped rather than failed, and both are exemptions that
# used to reach the log and not the grid. A platform whose sentence says it
# confines no writes has nothing for writable.outside to assert, and windows
# confines no filesystem in the fetch phase so there is no directory for
# writable.fetch.blobs to look for. The second of those had no branch at all --
# it fell through in silence on a lane the case is expected on, which is a hole
# that reads exactly like a lane that went quiet.

column1: # The environment scrub, from netinstall/test/envlen.sh. The same four lanes:
# the netinstall suite without a shorter list named for it, and envlen is in the
# reduced OpenBSD one too.
# This is the first suite here where a lane can be *unable* to make a claim
# rather than merely fail it, and three things decide that: whether the platform
# carries a 300-character name across execv, whether it carries 259, and whether
# it is windows -- whose scrub edits the environment block by hand and so shares
# neither the empty-name trigger nor the assigned-environ question.
# Every one of those branches reports. A section that cannot run emits a SKIP
# with its reason rather than falling through, so no cell here can be a hole,
# and the exemption is legible instead of being a lane name in an if. Measured
# both ways: the suite emits the same twenty-one ids on Linux and with the
# windows branches forced, five of them as skips on the second.
# envlen.trunc.keep255 is one id with two expectations, which is deliberate.
# Both branches read the same value; what differs is what the platform should
# have done with it -- a prefix that admits a long keeper must not truncate it,
# and windows admits no such prefix so neither name is one. That is one claim
# about one measurement, and splitting it would make the grid say two lanes
# tested different things when they tested the same thing.

column1: # What bounds a hostile host's bytes and seconds, from
# netinstall/test/fetchbound.sh. The same four lanes.
# The six fetchbound.fallback.* cases and fetchbound.stderr.guard are the branch
# where the kernel holds the bounds rather than curl, and it is reached only by a
# binary built -DNEUTRINO_FETCH_PREFER_WGET -- because every machine anyone can
# rent resolves curl. Until now that whole branch was simply absent from the
# grid rather than exempt from it: a lane that could not reach it said so in
# prose and filed nothing. They are skips with the reason on them now, so the
# difference between "this lane has no wget" and "this lane stopped reporting"
# is one the grid can show.
# windows-launch skips them for a second reason, and it is a better one: there
# is no fork and no setrlimit there, so nt_fetch is nt_win_spawn and no wget
